foundations-overview--docs.content:
import { Meta, Canvas } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import * as OverviewStories from './Overview.stories'

<Meta of={OverviewStories} />

# Foundations

Foundations are the decisions every component inherits: color, type,
spacing, radius, elevation, cursors, and the breakpoints layouts respond
to. They live in **one file** — `src/tokens.css` — as CSS custom
properties.

There is no JavaScript theme object and no `ThemeProvider` that owns
values. A token is a CSS variable, which means the platform already knows
how to scope it, cascade it, inherit it and override it. Everything on
this page follows from that.

`tokens.css` is itself generated — see [Where the values come
from](#where-the-values-come-from) — but nothing downstream of it is.
**You** consume a plain stylesheet with no build step of your own.

## The three layers

| Layer | Where | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Raw value | `:root` / `.dark` in `tokens.css` | `--primary: oklch(51.1% 0.262 276.966)` |
| Derived value | the `*` block in `tokens.css` | `--radius-control: max(…)` |
| Usage | a component's `.module.css` | `background: var(--primary)` |

Components only ever read the variable. That is what makes a rebrand a
change to one file, and what keeps theme conditionals out of component CSS
entirely — the value behind `var(--primary)` changes, the rule does not.

The derived layer is on `*` rather than `:root` on purpose: a custom
property that reads another one resolves where it is *declared*, so
putting these at the root would freeze them there and a `Theme` further
down the tree could not move them.

## Where the values come from

`tokens.css` is not written by hand. The source is a set of JSON files in
the [W3C design-token format](https://tr.designtokens.org/format/), and a
generator turns them into the stylesheet, the `Theme` component's list of
palettes, the swatches on the **Color** page, and an export for design
tools — four artefacts that used to be four chances to disagree with each
other.

Two things follow from that, and both are visible on other pages here.

**Nothing semantic holds a literal.** In the source, `primary` is
`{accent.solid}` and `foreground` is `{gray.950}` — references, not
colours. Swapping a ramp moves everything downstream of it in one edit,
which is what makes the 17 accents and 9 grays on this page a
three-line change rather than a rewrite.

**The contrast numbers are measured, not claimed.** For each of the 17
accents the generator converts the ramp through OKLCH → sRGB → relative
luminance, computes the contrast of each candidate step against a white
and a black label, and takes the first that clears 4.5:1. The focus ring
is a separate measurement against the page at 3:1. The lowest passing
accent in the current set sits at **4.56:1** — close enough to the floor
that guessing would have missed it.

Edit a ramp so that no step can carry a readable label and the build
stops with the hue named. The accessibility claims on the
[Color](?path=/docs/foundations-colors--docs) page are therefore checks,
not documentation.

## The pages

- **[Color](?path=/docs/foundations-colors--docs)** — semantic tokens, the
  contrast measurements, and where every value comes from.
- **[Dark mode](?path=/docs/foundations-dark-mode--docs)** — how the two
  modes are declared and switched.
- **[Typography](?path=/docs/foundations-typography--docs)** — the
  role-based type scale, and the system font stack behind it.
- **[Spacing](?path=/docs/foundations-spacing--docs)** — one multiplier,
  and why the scale cannot enforce itself.
- **[Breakpoints](?path=/docs/foundations-breakpoints--docs)** — the
  responsive range, and the kit's lack of opinion about it.
- **[Radius](?path=/docs/foundations-radius--docs)** — four steps off one
  base, and what happens at the extremes.
- **[Shadows](?path=/docs/foundations-shadows--docs)** — elevation, and why
  dark mode needs its own alphas.
- **[Cursors](?path=/docs/foundations-cursors--docs)** — two tokens and one
  contested convention.

## Theming

Overriding tokens globally is just CSS — redeclare them after Zweihänder's
stylesheet loads:

```css
:root {
  --radius: 1rem;
  --primary: oklch(0.55 0.2 264);
}
```

For anything narrower than the whole document, use `Theme`. It is a thin
wrapper that applies an appearance class and writes token overrides as
inline custom properties on one element, so everything inside it resolves
against those values.

```tsx
import { Theme } from 'zweihander/theme'

<Theme accentColor="violet" grayColor="slate" appearance="dark" radius="large" scaling="105%">
  <Button>Inside a violet, slate, dark, rounder, roomier scope</Button>
</Theme>
```

Five settings, each independent:

| Prop | Values |
| --- | --- |
| `accentColor` | 17 hues — drives `--primary` and `--ring` |
| `grayColor` | 9 neutral ramps — drives backgrounds, text, borders |
| `appearance` | `light`, `dark`, `inherit` |
| `radius` | `none`, `small`, `medium`, `large`, `full` |
| `scaling` | `90%` … `110%` — spacing and type together |

### Accent color

The brand hue. Seventeen, all of them measured: the solid step and the
label colour are chosen per hue so every accent clears 4.5:1 for its own
label, which is why the warm hues below carry dark labels and the cool
ones carry white. The focus ring uses a step darker than the fill, because
the lighter solids miss the 3:1 a focus indicator needs.

<Canvas of={OverviewStories.AccentColor} />

**`accentColor` sets `--primary`, not `--accent`.** The token named
`--accent` is a subtle hover surface — a different thing that happens to
share the word.

### Gray color

The neutral ramp behind surfaces, text, borders and muted fills. The
differences are subtle and cumulative; they read most clearly in dark
mode, which is how they are shown here.

<Canvas of={OverviewStories.GrayColor} />

### Scaling

One multiplier over both spacing and the type scale, so density is a
single setting rather than a per-component decision. Line heights are
unitless ratios and follow the font size on their own.

<Canvas of={OverviewStories.Scaling} />

Note that control heights scale too — at `90%` the default control is
36px, which is getting close to the floor for a touch target.

### Radius

Covered on its own page, including why `full` pills a button but not a
text field: **[Radius](?path=/docs/foundations-radius--docs)**.

### Appearance

`appearance` takes `light`, `dark`, or `inherit` (the default, which
leaves the surrounding mode alone).

<Canvas of={OverviewStories.Appearance} />

### Token overrides

`tokens` takes any custom property, with or without the `--` prefix. It is
not limited to tokens Zweihänder defines — the component writes whatever
you pass onto the element, so a token your own components read works the
same way.

<Canvas of={OverviewStories.TokenOverride} />

Overrides cascade, so a nested `Theme` inherits what it does not restate.
Because they are inline styles they also beat any stylesheet rule, which
is what makes a scoped override reliable — and what makes `Theme` the
wrong tool for setting global defaults. Use CSS for those.

### Nesting

Scopes nest in either direction: a dark panel on a light page, or a light
island inside a dark one.

<Canvas of={OverviewStories.Nested} />

The light island works because `tokens.css` declares the light values on
`:root, .light`, not on `:root` alone. `.dark` is declared afterwards at
equal specificity, so the nearer scope's class is what an element inside
it resolves against.

An `accentColor` or `grayColor` inside a nested scope follows the same
rule. Each appearance sets two switches, `--use-light` and `--use-dark`,
and the palette scopes pick their light or dark values through them, so
the nearest appearance wins at any depth, on the same element too.

<Canvas of={OverviewStories.NestedPalettes} />

**One caveat.** If your own CSS branches on theme with a descendant
selector (`.dark .thing { … }`), that selector still matches inside a
light island nested in a dark ancestor, and will style it as dark.
Zweihänder's own CSS never branches on theme, so it is unaffected. Read
the tokens instead of matching on `.dark` and the problem does not arise.

## Installing

Both distribution paths carry the same tokens. Copy-source drops the
component's own source into your repo and merges these values into your
stylesheet; the npm package ships them as `zweihander/tokens.css`, which
you import after your base stylesheet.

The exact commands for either are in the
[repo README](https://github.com/nguucode/zweihander).

foundations-colors--docs.content:
import { Meta, Canvas } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import * as ColorsStories from './Colors.stories'

<Meta of={ColorsStories} />

# Colors

Every color in the system is a CSS custom property declared in
`src/tokens.css`, with a counterpart under the `.dark` class. There is no
separate dark palette file and no JS theme object — one stylesheet holds
both modes.

**Read them with `var()`** — `background: var(--card)`,
`color: var(--muted-foreground)`, `border-color: var(--border)`. Because
the variable changes rather than the rule, a component written this way
switches theme without a single conditional: there is no light branch and
no dark branch anywhere in the kit's CSS.

**The swatches below read their values out of the live document**, so a
color shown here is the value the components actually get. The token
*names* are still listed by hand in `Colors.stories.tsx`, though — add a
token to `tokens.css` and it will not appear here until it is added there
too.

## Surfaces

`--background` is the page. `--card` and `--popover` are surfaces that sit
a level above it — a card inset in the page, a menu floating over it. In
light mode all three are pure white and only their foregrounds carry
meaning; in dark mode they separate, with `--background` at the darkest
step and card/popover lifted one step toward the viewer.

Each surface has a `-foreground` partner, and the pair is the contract:
put `--card-foreground` on `--card`, never `--foreground`, even where the
two happen to be equal today.

<Canvas of={ColorsStories.Surfaces} />

## Subtle surfaces

`--muted` and `--accent` are the same value in both modes and differ only
in intent. `--muted` is for surfaces that recede — a disabled field's
fill, a table's zebra stripe — and is the only one of the two with a
foreground meant for *long-form* secondary text. `--accent` is for
surfaces that are reacting to the user: hover on a menu item, the
selected row in a list.

They are interchangeable in appearance, so nothing breaks visually if you
swap them, and nothing tells you that you did. The distinction is the
whole point: when a brand color eventually replaces one of them, only the
intent that should change will change.

<Canvas of={ColorsStories.SubtleSurfaces} />

## Solid actions

Filled controls. `--primary` is the default button and **the brand hue** —
indigo out of the box, and the one token the
[`accentColor`](?path=/docs/foundations-overview--docs) setting moves. It
lightens in dark mode rather than darkening, so `--primary-foreground`
inverts with it.

`--destructive` is a hue too, but a fixed one: it stays red whatever the
accent is. A status colour that follows the brand stops being a status —
if the accent is already red, distinguish destructive actions by wording
and placement, not by colour alone.

A note on names: the token called `--accent` is **not** the brand hue. It
is a subtle surface (hover, selected row). The brand hue is `--primary`.
The collision is unfortunate and predates this kit — the names come from
the token contract the registry is compatible with.

<Canvas of={ColorsStories.SolidActions} />

## Lines and focus

`--border` is a divider or a container edge, `--input` is a form control's
edge, `--ring` is the focus indicator. None of them take a foreground —
they are only ever an outline color, never a fill behind text.

`--border` and `--input` are the same value in both modes and, like
muted/accent, are separated by intent rather than appearance. In dark mode
they stop being opaque neutrals and become white at 10% and 15% alpha
respectively, so an edge reads consistently whether it sits on
`--background` or on a lifted `--card`. That is the one place the palette
uses transparency.

<Canvas of={ColorsStories.LinesAndFocus} />

## Dark mode

Every token on this page has a counterpart under `.dark`, switched by a
class rather than a media query, and dark is not a mechanical inversion of
light — surfaces go *up* rather than down, and strong fills get lighter so
their foregrounds flip to dark text. The Light/Dark columns in the
contrast table below cover both.

The mechanism, the three places an inversion would have gone wrong, and
how to follow the OS setting are on their own page:
**[Dark mode](?path=/docs/foundations-dark-mode--docs)**.

## Contrast

Measured, not assumed — every pair below is computed from the OKLCH
values in `tokens.css`. WCAG AA wants 4.5:1 for body text and 3:1 for UI
component boundaries such as a focus ring.

| Pair | Light | Dark |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `background` / `foreground` | 19.79:1 | 18.96:1 |
| `card` / `card-foreground` | 19.79:1 | 17.16:1 |
| `popover` / `popover-foreground` | 19.79:1 | 17.16:1 |
| `primary` / `primary-foreground` | 6.17:1 | 5.74:1 |
| `secondary` / `secondary-foreground` | 16.42:1 | 14.48:1 |
| `accent` / `accent-foreground` | 16.42:1 | 14.48:1 |
| `destructive` / `destructive-foreground` | 4.56:1 | 6.19:1 |
| `muted` / `muted-foreground` | 4.60:1 | 5.83:1 |
| `background` / `muted-foreground` | 5.02:1 | 7.63:1 |
| `background` / `ring` | 8.07:1 | 6.34:1 |

The `primary` row is the default indigo accent. Every one of the seventeen
accents is measured the same way and clears 4.5:1 for its own label — see
[Overview → Accent color](?path=/docs/foundations-overview--docs).

**`--muted-foreground` on `--muted` is 4.60:1 in light mode**, the
tightest pair it forms. It used to be 4.34:1, under AA: gray-500 on every
ramp has since been darkened to the lightest value that clears 4.6:1 on
its own gray-100, so muted text can now sit on a muted fill. On the page background, where secondary
text usually lives, the same token is 5.02:1.

**`--surface-subtle` is a filled panel that muted text can sit on.**
Muted text reads 4.81:1 on it (gray-50, neutral) and 5.83:1 on gray-800 in dark — a step off `--card` so a filled panel still reads as filled. The build
measures `--muted-foreground` on `--background`, `--card`,
`--surface-subtle` and `--muted` in both modes on all nine gray ramps, and
stops if any pair drops under 4.5:1. The tightest is neutral on `--muted`,
at 4.60:1.

**`--control-border` outlines a checkbox, radio or switch track.** Those
controls have nothing else that shows they are there, so WCAG 1.4.11 wants
3:1 against the page — and `--input` (gray-200) is about 1.3:1. The build
measures it on all nine gray ramps.

**`--primary-text` is the brand hue as text** — an outlined or ghost
primary button. The solid is picked for its label, not for being read on
the page, and amber-500 on white is barely 2:1, so the build measures a
third step per accent that clears 4.5:1 against the page.

**Two values are deliberately off the beaten path.** `--ring` follows the
accent at its `-700` step rather than being a neutral, because a focus
indicator has to clear 3:1 against the page under WCAG 1.4.11 and the
lighter solids miss it — yellow-600 measures 2.93:1, so the ring uses a
step darker than the fill for every accent.
And dark `--destructive-foreground` is neutral-900 rather than near-white:
dark mode inverts the destructive fill to red-400, and near-white on
red-400 is 2.77:1, which makes the label of a destructive button in dark
mode fail AA outright.

## Status

Four fixed hues for messages about state: `info` (blue), `success`
(green), `warning` (amber), `danger` (red). Like `--destructive`, they do
not follow the accent. Each comes as four tokens:

| Token | Use | Light | Dark |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `--{status}` | Solid fill | 600 (green 700, amber 500) | 400 |
| `--{status}-foreground` | Label on the solid | neutral-50 (amber: neutral-900) | neutral-900 |
| `--{status}-subtle` | Tinted fill | 100 | 950 |
| `--{status}-text` | Text, icon and border on the tint or the page | 800 | 300 |

The steps are pinned by hand, so `npm run tokens` measures them and fails
the build if any pair drops under 4.5:1:

| Pair | info | success | warning | danger |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| label on solid, light | 5.03:1 | 4.73:1 | 8.35:1 | 4.56:1 |
| text on subtle, light | 7.25:1 | 6.45:1 | 6.41:1 | 6.86:1 |
| text on page, light | 8.84:1 | 7.09:1 | 7.13:1 | 8.37:1 |
| label on solid, dark | 6.79:1 | 10.09:1 | 10.43:1 | 6.19:1 |
| text on subtle, dark | 8.13:1 | 10.67:1 | 10.37:1 | 8.40:1 |
| text on page, dark | 10.93:1 | 14.16:1 | 13.69:1 | 10.30:1 |

`danger` and `destructive` share red-600 but mean different things:
`destructive` is an action that destroys, `danger` is a state that is
wrong. Keep them apart so either can move without the other.

## Color is never the only signal

`--destructive` on a button does not say what will be destroyed, and a red
badge means nothing to a reader who cannot distinguish it from a neutral
one. Pair color with words, an icon, or a shape every time it carries
meaning. The contrast numbers above are a floor, not a design review.

## Where the values come from

**Every value is a step off a published ramp, digit for digit.** Nothing
here was hand-picked or eyeballed. Two ramps feed the palette and each is
swappable on its own: an **accent** (indigo by default) for `--primary` and
`--ring`, and a **gray** (neutral by default) for everything structural.

| Token | Light | Dark | Driven by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `background` | white | gray-950 | gray |
| `foreground` | gray-950 | gray-50 | gray |
| `card`, `popover` | white | gray-900 | gray |
| `card-foreground`, `popover-foreground` | gray-950 | gray-50 | gray |
| `primary` | accent-600 | accent-400 | **accent** |
| `primary-foreground` | white or near-black | near-black | **accent** |
| `secondary`, `muted`, `accent` | gray-100 | gray-800 | gray |
| `secondary-foreground`, `accent-foreground` | gray-900 | gray-50 | gray |
| `muted-foreground` | gray-500 | gray-400 | gray |
| `surface-subtle` | gray-50 | gray-800 | gray |
| `destructive` | red-600 | red-400 | fixed |
| `destructive-foreground` | neutral-50 | neutral-900 | fixed |
| `border`, `input` | gray-200 | white 10% / 15% | gray |
| `control-border` | gray-500 | gray-400 | gray |
| `ring` | accent-700 | accent-400 | **accent** |
| `primary-text` | first of accent-600…900 at 4.5:1 on white | first of accent-400…200 at 4.5:1 on the dark page | **accent** |

The light accent step is `-600` for most hues but `-700` for sky, fuchsia,
pink and rose, and the label is white or near-black depending on which one
clears 4.5:1 on that fill — the warm hues take dark labels. Exceptions to
the ramp rule: light `--background` (pure white, not gray-50) and dark
`--border`/`--input` (alpha, so edges work over any surface).

`--destructive` deliberately does **not** follow the accent. A status
colour that changes with the brand stops being a status.

## Naming

Token names describe a **role**, not a property or a color. `--primary` is
not "the brand color" and `--destructive` is not "red"; they are the
default action and the dangerous one. The names are also the common
contract most token-based kits share, which is what lets a component
copied out of Zweihänder resolve against tokens a target project already
has instead of arriving with its own private palette.

Figma, by contrast, conventionally names tokens by property —
`bg/primary`, `text/primary`, `border/default`. Those do not map one to
one: Figma's `text/primary` is this system's `--foreground`, and its
`bg/primary` is `--background`. Neither is `--primary`. Worth pinning down
before any Figma sync, since the collision is silent.

## Primitives

The full underlying palette — 22 hues × 11 shades. None of these
classes are referenced anywhere in the kit, so they are force-generated by
an `@source inline(...)` directive in `src/index.css` purely so this page
can render them.

This is raw material, not a palette to build UI from. Reach for a
primitive when you are defining the *next* semantic token; if a primitive
shows up in a component, a token is missing.

<Canvas of={ColorsStories.Primitives} />

## Customization

Swap the raw values in `:root` and `.dark` in `src/tokens.css`. Nothing
that reads `var(--primary)` or `var(--muted-foreground)` changes, because
every rule points at the variable rather than the value.

Two things to carry through a rebrand: re-measure the pairs in the
contrast table — a brand hue at the same *lightness* as neutral-900 will
not necessarily hit the same ratios — and keep light and dark as separate
decisions. Lifting a brand color for dark mode by reusing the light value
is what produces the 2.77:1 failure documented above.

Projects that install through the registry get these values merged into
their own stylesheet; projects on the npm package import
`zweihander/tokens.css` and override afterwards.

import { Meta, Canvas } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import * as DarkModeStories from './DarkMode.stories'

<Meta of={DarkModeStories} />

# Dark mode

Dark mode is **a class, not a media query.** `tokens.css` declares the
light values on `:root, .light` and the dark values on `.dark`, and
Every rule in the kit reads those variables, so the class is the only
switch there is.

Nothing is automatic about it. Adding `class="dark"` to `<html>` is what
switches the document; without that, a device set to dark mode gets the
light theme. That is the trade — see **Following the system** below.

<Canvas of={DarkModeStories.SideBySide} />

## Components don't know about it

No component stylesheet — `Button.module.css`, `InputField.module.css` or any other — mentions `.dark`.
They write `background: var(--primary)`, and it is the variable that
changes; the rule is identical in both modes.

This is the main reason to reach for a token rather than a literal. A
hard-coded `#0a0a0a` is near-black in both modes and needs a `.dark`
override beside it to survive a theme switch; `var(--primary)` needs
nothing. Every theme conditional in a codebase is a place a value was
hardcoded and then patched.

## Dark is not an inversion

Flipping lightness would produce the wrong result in three places, and the
palette deliberately doesn't:

- **`--background` is neutral-950, not black.** A pure-black page makes
  the halation around light text worse and leaves no room to sit a surface
  *below* the page level.
- **Surfaces go up, not down.** `--card` and `--popover` are a step
  *lighter* than the page in dark mode and identical to it in light mode.
  Elevation in dark mode is carried by lightness, because a drop shadow
  has almost nothing left to darken (see
  [Shadows](?path=/docs/foundations-shadows--docs)).
- **Strong fills become light, so their labels become dark.**
  `--primary` goes from near-black to near-white, and
  `--primary-foreground` inverts with it. `--destructive` does the same,
  red-600 to red-400 — which is exactly where the palette's one contrast
  bug lived: keeping the near-white label on the lightened red measured
  2.77:1. It is now neutral-900 at 6.19:1. Inverting a fill without
  inverting its foreground is the single easiest dark-mode mistake to
  make.

Full measurements for both modes are in
[Color → Contrast](?path=/docs/foundations-colors--docs).

## Alpha for edges

`--border` and `--input` are the one place the palette uses transparency:
opaque neutral-200 in light, `white / 10%` and `white / 15%` in dark. An
opaque dark border would have to be re-chosen for every surface it sits
on; a translucent white edge lightens whatever is underneath, so the same
token reads correctly on `--background` and on a lifted `--card`.

## Scoping

`Theme` switches an appearance for a subtree rather than the document —
a dark footer on a light page, a light popover inside a dark shell. See
[Overview → Nesting](?path=/docs/foundations-overview--docs) for how the
nesting resolves and the one caveat that comes with it.

```tsx
<Theme appearance="dark">
  <Footer />
</Theme>
```

## Following the system

The kit ships no `prefers-color-scheme` handling, because the choice
between "follow the OS" and "remember what the user picked" belongs to the
app, not the component library. The usual shape:

```ts
const media = window.matchMedia('(prefers-color-scheme: dark)')
const stored = localStorage.getItem('theme') // 'light' | 'dark' | null
const dark = stored ? stored === 'dark' : media.matches
document.documentElement.classList.toggle('dark', dark)
```

Two things worth getting right. Run it **before first paint** — in a
blocking inline script in `<head>`, not in a `useEffect` — or the page
renders light and flips, which is the flash every themed site has had at
some point. And keep listening to `media` afterwards so a user changing
their OS setting mid-session is followed, unless they have made an
explicit choice.

In this Storybook, the **Theme** toolbar control does the class toggle for
you; there is no persistence and no system detection.

import { Meta, Canvas } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import * as TypographyStories from './Typography.stories'

<Meta of={TypographyStories} />

# Typography

Type is **role-based**: you reach for `--text-heading-lg` or `--text-body`,
not a size. Each role carries its size, line height and weight together, so a
heading cannot end up at body weight or a body line height by omission.

The alternative — a purely dimensional scale, where a name says how big and
never what it is for — is what this replaces. Each role is three variables
that belong together:

```css
.heading {
  font-size: var(--text-heading-lg);
  line-height: var(--leading-heading-lg);
  font-weight: 700;
}
```

## The typeface

`--font-sans` leads with **`system-ui`**:

```css
system-ui, -apple-system, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, 'Helvetica Neue', Arial,
sans-serif, 'Apple Color Emoji', 'Segoe UI Emoji'
```

`system-ui` is the standards-track keyword, and it resolves to the
platform's **UI** face — San Francisco on Apple platforms, Segoe UI
Variable on Windows, Roboto on Android — which is the face those platforms
use for their own controls. Everything after it is a fallback for browsers
that do not support the keyword.

<Canvas of={TypographyStories.Families} />

**The known caveat.** On some Linux and older Android configurations
`system-ui` resolves through fontconfig to whatever is aliased as the
system font, which has historically produced a serif, or a
missing-glyph fallback for non-Latin text. The rest of the stack does not
rescue it, because the keyword *did* resolve — just badly. This is the
reason some systems leave `system-ui` out of the stack entirely. If you
ship to those platforms and see the wrong face, drop it from the front;
nothing else in the kit depends on it.

Nothing is downloaded, so the kit renders in a different face on every
platform by design. That is the right default for product UI and the wrong
one for a brand with its own type — see **Customization** below.

## Headings

Seven steps, all bold. The line height tightens as the size grows, which
is the thing a single ratio applied across a whole scale gets wrong.

<Canvas of={TypographyStories.Headings} />

| Role | Size | Line height |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--text-heading-2xl` | 2rem / 32px | 36px |
| `--text-heading-xl` | 1.75rem / 28px | 32px |
| `--text-heading-lg` | 1.5rem / 24px | 28px |
| `--text-heading-md` | 1.25rem / 20px | 24px |
| `--text-heading-sm` | 1rem / 16px | 20px |
| `--text-heading-xs` | 0.875rem / 14px | 20px |
| `--text-heading-2xs` | 0.75rem / 12px | 16px |

Note that headings go *below* body size: `--text-heading-2xs` is 12px. Those
bottom steps are for labels and section eyebrows — a heading role is about
the semantic weight of the text, not about being large.

## Body

Three steps. `--text-body` is the default at 14px — one step down from the
16px a lot of interfaces start at, which is deliberate for dense product
UI and worth knowing before you reach for it in long-form content.

<Canvas of={TypographyStories.Body} />

| Role | Size | Line height |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--text-body-lg` | 1rem / 16px | 24px |
| `--text-body` | 0.875rem / 14px | 20px |
| `--text-body-sm` | 0.75rem / 12px | 16px |

**Every component uses these.** Button, the field label, the input itself,
and the helper and error text are all `--text-body`; only the large Button
steps up to `--text-body-lg`.

## Weights

Four. Anything outside this set is not part of the system.

<Canvas of={TypographyStories.Weights} />

| Weight | Value |
| --- | --- |
| regular | 400 |
| medium | 500 |
| semibold | 600 |
| bold | 700 |

Weight is written directly rather than tokenised — there are four of them
and they are the same four everywhere, so a `--font-weight-medium`
indirection would buy nothing. Button is `--text-body` at `font-weight:
500`; the role supplies the size and line height, the rule supplies the
weight.

With a system stack, the weight you ask for is not guaranteed to be a
drawn face: where one is missing the browser synthesises it, and
synthesised weights look noticeably worse. 400 and 500 are safe
everywhere; verify 600 on the platforms you support.

## Scaling

Every size above is `calc(<base> * var(--scaling))`, so the
[`scaling`](?path=/docs/foundations-overview--docs) setting moves type and
spacing together. Line heights are stored as *ratios* — `calc(20 / 14)`
rather than `1.25rem` — so they follow the font size instead of having to
be rescaled themselves.

## What is not here

**A metric role for large figures.** Its sizes would be identical to three
of the heading steps; the real difference is tabular figures, which
`font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` already covers. There is no stat
component yet, so it would be a role nothing reads.

**A code role.** Same size as `--text-body-sm`, differing only by family.
`var(--font-mono)` covers it until a Code component exists.

## Customization

The family is a token like any other:

```css
:root {
  --font-sans: 'Inter Variable', system-ui, sans-serif;
}
```

Every rule that reads `var(--font-sans)` picks it up with no component
change — which is all of them, because components set the family
explicitly rather than inheriting it from the page. Re-check the weights when you do — a real typeface
usually ships fewer weights than the four above, or different ones.

To move the scale itself rather than the face, override the role tokens
directly — each is a `--text-<role>` and its `--leading-<role>` partner.

foundations-spacing--docs.content:
import { Meta, Canvas } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import * as SpacingStories from './Spacing.stories'

<Meta of={SpacingStories} />

# Spacing

The entire spacing system is **one number**. `--spacing` is `0.25rem`
(4px), and every spacing utility multiplies it: `p-4` is
`calc(var(--spacing) * 4)` — 16px. There is no list of allowed values
anywhere in `tokens.css`, because there is no list.

## The scale is computed, not enumerated

This is the part that differs from most design systems. Where a scale is
a fixed map, `p-13` is an error because 13 is not in it. Here the value
is computed, so `p-13` (52px), `p-4.5` (18px) and `p-[7px]` all work.

That has a real consequence: **the scale cannot enforce itself.** Nothing
will stop a component from using `gap-7` where the rest of the kit uses
`gap-6`; there is no build error, no lint failure, and the result looks
almost right. The steps shown below are a convention the team keeps, not a
constraint the tooling applies.

<Canvas of={SpacingStories.Scale} />

Steps below `1` exist and are worth knowing: `0.5` (2px) and `1.5` (6px)
are what you reach for between a label and its input, or an icon and its
label — gaps where a full 4px reads as a break rather than a pairing.

## What the kit uses

Every component here stays on whole steps, and on a small set of them:

| Step | Used for |
| --- | --- |
| `1.5` (6px) | gap between a field label, its input and its helper text |
| `2` (8px) | gap between a button's icon and its label |
| `3` (12px) | horizontal padding, small button and all inputs |
| `4` (16px) | horizontal padding, default button |
| `6` (24px) | horizontal padding, large button |
| `8` / `10` / `12` (32 / 40 / 48px) | the three control heights |

The control heights are the load-bearing ones. A 40px default (`h-10`) is
what makes a button and a text input line up in a row without either
being nudged, and anything that should sit alongside them — a select, a
date picker — has to land on the same three heights rather than pick its
own.

## Customization

Change `--spacing` in `src/tokens.css` and the whole system rescales at
once. Setting it to `0.2rem` makes every gap, pad and control height in
the kit 20% tighter with no other edit.

Two cautions. Control heights rescale with everything else, so a tighter
`--spacing` shrinks the tap targets too — 40px is already close to the
44px minimum recommended for touch, and much below it becomes an
accessibility problem rather than a density preference. And because the
base is in `rem`, every value inherits the user's root font size; that is
the behaviour you want, but it means "40px" is only 40px at the default
16px root.

import { Meta, Canvas } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import * as BreakpointsStories from './Breakpoints.stories'

<Meta of={BreakpointsStories} />

# Breakpoints

Five breakpoints, inherited from the underlying CSS framework without
modification. Zweihänder declares no `--breakpoint-*` of its own.

| Prefix | Min width | At a 16px root |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *(none)* | `0` | 0px |
| `sm:` | `40rem` | 640px |
| `md:` | `48rem` | 768px |
| `lg:` | `64rem` | 1024px |
| `xl:` | `80rem` | 1280px |
| `2xl:` | `96rem` | 1536px |

<Canvas of={BreakpointsStories.Scale} />

The box below reports the breakpoint currently in effect. Resize the
preview — or use Storybook's viewport toolbar — and it changes.

<Canvas of={BreakpointsStories.Active} />

## They are min-width, and that has a direction

`md:flex` means "flex at 768px **and above**". There is no maximum, so
rules outside a media query are the small-screen case and every
`@media (width >= …)` is an override for larger screens. Write the phone
layout first and widen it; writing the desktop layout first means every
breakpoint has to undo something.

The other direction is expressible — `@media (width < 48rem)` caps a rule
below a breakpoint — but mixing both in one component is where responsive
CSS usually becomes unreadable. Pick min-width and stay there.

## Breakpoints are in rem

`40rem`, not `640px`. A reader who raises their browser's default font
size gets the layout to break earlier, because the layout responds to how
large the text actually is rather than to the device. That is the correct
behaviour and it is worth not overriding: a `px` breakpoint holds a
multi-column layout together long after its text has stopped fitting.

The px column above is only true at the default 16px root.

## The kit has no opinion yet

**No component here uses a breakpoint.** Controls such as Button and Text
Input are inline-sized — they fill whatever their container gives them and have no
layout of their own to rearrange. The stories on this page are the only
responsive code in the repo.

That is expected at this stage: breakpoints are a **layout** concern, and
layout is the [Patterns](?path=/docs/patterns-overview--docs) tier, which
is empty. Marketing sections, dashboards and checkout flows are where
these will actually get used, and where the kit will need an opinion about
which of the five are load-bearing. Most design systems end up leaning on
two or three.

## Container queries are usually the better tool

A breakpoint asks how wide the *viewport* is. A component almost always
wants to know how wide **its own container** is — the same card is narrow
in a sidebar and wide in a main column at one identical viewport width.

Container queries are in every current browser, and they are plain CSS:

```css
.card {
  container-type: inline-size;
}

.cardBody {
  display: flex;
  flex-direction: column;
}

@container (width >= 28rem) {
  .cardBody {
    flex-direction: row;
  }
}
```

When a component is built here that needs to reflow, it should reach for
`@container` first and a viewport breakpoint only when the thing being
arranged really is the page.

## Customization

Breakpoints are theme keys like any other, redefined in the `@theme`
block:

```css
@theme {
  --breakpoint-sm: 30rem;
  --breakpoint-3xl: 120rem;
}
```

Two cautions. These generate utility *variants*, so they cannot be
overridden per-scope by `Theme` the way a color can — a variant is
compiled into a media query at build time, and there is no runtime
variable to swap. And removing a default breakpoint removes its prefix
entirely, so any existing `lg:` becomes a silent no-op rather than an
error.

import { Meta, Canvas } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import * as RadiusStories from './Radius.stories'

<Meta of={RadiusStories} />

# Radius

Rounding is a **single setting**, not a value picked per component. A
`radius` preset on `Theme` rescales everything inside it at once, and
components follow because they reference an *intent* — control, field,
panel — rather than a fixed number.

```tsx
<Theme radius="large">
  <Button>Rounder</Button>
</Theme>
```

## Presets

Five: `none`, `small`, **`medium` (the default)**, `large`, `full`. The
default is set by `--radius-factor: 1` and `--radius-full: 0px` on
`:root`, which is exactly what the `medium` preset writes — so a scope
with no `radius` prop and a scope with `radius="medium"` are identical.

<Canvas of={RadiusStories.Presets} />

Look at the `full` row. **The button becomes a pill; the input and the
panel get rounder but stop short of one.** That is the whole reason this
is a system rather than a number: a fully rounded text field reads as a
search pill in a form that isn't one, and a fully rounded card stops
looking like a container. Only controls opt all the way in.

`none` flattens every corner in the scope to `0`, including panels.

## How it works

Two variables do the work, both on `:root`:

| Variable | Default | Set by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--radius` | `0.625rem` | you, for the base step |
| `--radius-factor` | `1` | the `radius` preset |
| `--radius-full` | `0px` | the `radius` preset, only at `full` |

Every step is the base multiplied by the factor, so the preset scales the
whole scale rather than replacing it:

| Preset | Factor | `--radius-full` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `none` | `0` | `0px` |
| `small` | `0.5` | `0px` |
| `medium` | `1` | `0px` |
| `large` | `1.5` | `0px` |
| `full` | `1.5` | `9999px` |

The pill is a `max()`. `--radius-control` resolves to
`max(step, var(--radius-full))` — normally the step wins because
`--radius-full` is `0px`, and at the `full` preset the `9999px` wins
instead.

Fields and panels use the same shape with a ceiling wrapped around it:

```css
max(step, min(cap, var(--radius-full)))
```

`min(cap, --radius-full)` is `0px` normally and the cap at `full`, so they
step up with the preset and stop there. Concretely, at the default base:

| Preset | `control` | `field` | `panel` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `none` | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| `small` | 4px | 4px | 5px |
| `medium` | 8px | 8px | 10px |
| `large` | 12px | 12px | 15px |
| `full` | pill | 15px | 21px |

The input is 40px tall, so a pill would be 20px — `field` at `full` lands
under that on purpose, and a test asserts it.

## Intent tokens

What components actually use.

<Canvas of={RadiusStories.Intent} />

| Token | Used by | Pills at `full` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--radius-control` | Button, and future badges/chips | yes |
| `--radius-field` | TextInput, and future textareas/selects | no |
| `--radius-panel` | future cards, dialogs, popovers | no |

A new component should pick the intent that matches its shape, not a step.
Getting this wrong is invisible at the default preset and only shows up
when someone sets `radius="full"` — which is exactly the kind of bug a
token system exists to prevent.

## Steps

The raw scale — `--radius-sm` through `--radius-xl` — for anything that is
genuinely decorative rather than a control, field or panel.

<Canvas of={RadiusStories.Steps} />

These follow the preset like everything else, so a decorative corner in
application code stays in step with the controls beside it.

A genuinely circular element — an avatar, a status dot — should use
`border-radius: 50%` rather than a token. `--radius-full` is the pill
switch, not a "make this round" value: read directly it is `0` at every
preset except `full`.

## Scoping and overriding

Presets nest, and `Theme` takes a `render` prop, so a single component can
opt out without a wrapper element:

```tsx
<Theme radius="full" render={<Button />}>
  Just this one is a pill
</Theme>
```

For a value the presets don't cover, set the variables directly — `tokens`
is applied after the preset, so it wins:

```tsx
<Theme radius="large" tokens={{ 'radius-factor': '2.4' }}>
```

Globally, change the base in CSS and leave the factor to the presets:

```css
:root {
  --radius: 1rem;
}
```

## One caveat about the base

The steps are offsets from the base — `sm` is `base − 4px`, not
`base × 0.6` — so a base far below the default degenerates. At
`--radius: 0.25rem` (4px) the steps are `0 / 2 / 4 / 8px` and `sm`
collapses to a square corner.

The factor does not have this problem, because it multiplies the finished
step. Prefer moving the preset over moving the base, and if the base does
need to change substantially, switch the four `calc()`s in `tokens.css`
from offsets to ratios.

import { Meta, Canvas } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import * as ShadowsStories from './Shadows.stories'

<Meta of={ShadowsStories} />

# Shadows

Seven elevation steps and an off switch. They read as `var(--shadow-2xs)`
through `var(--shadow-2xl)`, and each resolves per appearance rather than
being a fixed value.

<Canvas of={ShadowsStories.Scale} />

## The scale is one shape at seven heights

A step is not a blur radius someone liked. Each one is a **height `h`**,
and both of its layers fall out of that number:

```
ambient  0  h     2h    -h/2     the spread of light around a raised object
contact  0  h/2   h     -h/2     the tighter dark where it meets the surface
```

Two layers because one cannot do both jobs. A single soft shadow floats
without touching down; a single tight one reads as a border. The negative
spread pulls both layers in as they rise, which is what keeps a tall step
from bleeding sideways into whatever sits next to it.

| Token | h | Light |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--shadow-none` | — | `0 0 #0000` |
| `--shadow-2xs` | 1 | 1px drop, 5% |
| `--shadow-xs` | 2 | 2px + 1px, 6% / 4% |
| `--shadow-sm` | 4 | 4px + 2px, 8% / 5% |
| `--shadow-md` | 8 | 8px + 4px, 9% / 6% |
| `--shadow-lg` | 12 | 12px + 6px, 10% / 7% |
| `--shadow-xl` | 20 | 20px + 10px, 12% / 8% |
| `--shadow-2xl` | 32 | 32px + 16px, 16% / 10% |

`h` doubles through the lower steps and eases off at the top, because the
difference between 1px and 2px of lift is legible and the difference
between 40px and 48px is not.

`--shadow-none` exists so that turning elevation off is a token rather
than a literal. `box-shadow: none` also works, but it cannot be swapped by
a `Theme` and it breaks a transition between two shadow states — `0 0
#0000` interpolates, `none` does not.

## Dark mode is derived, not retyped

Only the light values are written down. The dark ones are **computed from
them**: every alpha is multiplied by 4 and clamped at 0.6.

<Canvas of={ShadowsStories.Modes} />

Look at the dark half. The shadows are nearly invisible, and multiplying
the alpha by four is not what fixes it — nothing fixes it. Here is the
measurement, sampling the darkest pixel each shadow can produce:

| | Page | Darkest shadow pixel | Range |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Light, `--shadow-md` | 255 | 232 | **23 levels** |
| Light, `--shadow-2xl` | 255 | 214 | **41 levels** |
| Dark, `--shadow-md` | 10 | 6 | **4 levels** |
| Dark, `--shadow-2xl` | 10 | 4 | **6 levels** |

A drop shadow works by darkening what is under it. The dark page is
already at 10 of 255, so **the entire budget is 10 levels** — even a
pure-black shadow at full opacity could not do better. Light mode has 255
to spend. That is a 25× difference in available range, and no choice of
alpha closes it.

So the multiplier is not rescuing dark mode; it is spending a small budget
well rather than leaving it unspent. What actually carries elevation in
dark mode is the surface: `--card` sits at **23** against a background of
**10**, a 13-level lift — two to three times stronger than any shadow on
this page.

**In dark mode, surface lightness is the primary elevation signal and the
shadow is a secondary cue.** In light mode it is the other way around. If
you are building a floating surface and it does not read as raised in dark
mode, reach for a lighter surface token, not a heavier shadow.

The **clamp** at 0.6 is therefore housekeeping rather than tuning — it
stops a large light alpha from generating a nonsensical dark one, and
between `--shadow-2xl` uncapped and capped there is about one level in it.

Deriving rather than retyping closes a different gap. When both modes were
written by hand there were fourteen numbers and nothing checking that they
told the same story; editing a step meant remembering to edit its twin.
Now editing a step edits both, and the `Modes` story asserts the two did
not collapse into the same value — set the multiplier to 1 and that test
fails.

## Who uses them

Controls are flat: Button, Text Input and the rest carry borders, not
shadows. **Card** is the first surface on the scale — `elevated` rests on
`--shadow-sm` and lifts to `--shadow-md` on hover when clickable. The
remaining steps are for the surfaces still to come (popover, dropdown,
modal, toast), documented now so they adopt a shared scale instead of each
inventing a `box-shadow`.

That also means the steps are **untested against real components.** The
geometry is consistent, but consistent is not the same as tuned. Treat
them as a starting point to adjust when the first floating surface lands.

## A note on rings and shadows

`box-shadow` is a single property, so a shadow and a focus ring drawn the
same way would overwrite each other — which is why systems that draw rings
with `box-shadow` need machinery to compose the two.

The kit sidesteps it: focus is drawn with `outline`, which has its own
property and its own `outline-offset`, and current browsers follow
`border-radius` with it. An elevated surface can carry a shadow and a
focus ring at once, and neither needs to know about the other.

## What is not here

**Inset shadows.** For recessed wells and pressed states. They are a real
gap, but the kit has no recessed surface and no pressed treatment yet, so
they would be a step nothing reads — and this page already carries seven
of those. Add them as `elevation-inset-*` in `tokens/semantic.json` when
the first one lands; the alpha derivation applies unchanged.

**Coloured shadows.** A shadow tinted toward the accent instead of black.
Worth having, but it needs a real decision about which token it reads and
how it behaves in dark mode, not a mechanical port.

## Customization

The raw values are `--elevation-none` through `--elevation-2xl` in `:root`
and `.dark`; the `*` block maps them onto `--shadow-*` and does not need to
change.

Change a step by editing `tokens/semantic.json` and running `npm run
tokens` — light and dark regenerate together. Overriding `--shadow-md`
directly on a `Theme` scope also works and skips the derivation, which is
the right tool for a one-off surface and the wrong one for changing the
scale.

foundations-cursors--docs.content:
import { Meta, Canvas } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import * as CursorsStories from './Cursors.stories'

<Meta of={CursorsStories} />

# Cursors

Three tokens, and a convention that surprises most people: **buttons do
not get `cursor: pointer`. Links do.**

## The convention

`cursor: pointer` means "this navigates" — it is the hand that appears
over a link. Browsers have never applied it to `<button>`, `<select>` or a
checkbox, and neither does this kit. Interactive elements that act on the
current page keep the regular arrow; only a link gets the hand. This is a
deliberate departure from the very common `button { cursor: pointer }`
reset.

It is worth knowing the argument on the other side: a large body of
usability opinion holds that the hand cursor is now such a widespread
affordance for "clickable" that removing it costs more than the semantic
purity gains. If your product takes that view, this is a one-line change —
see **Customization** below. The point of making it a token is that it is
one line, in one place, rather than a decision re-litigated per component.

<Canvas of={CursorsStories.Tokens} />

## `--cursor-button`

`default` — the regular arrow. Applied by Button.

Note this changes nothing visually today: a native `<button>` already
shows the arrow. **The token's job is not its current value; it is that
the value is reachable.** Without it, switching the kit to `pointer` means
editing every component; with it, it is one declaration.

## `--cursor-link`

`pointer` — the hand.

This one exists because the convention above has a second half that is
easy to state and easy to get wrong. Button takes `href`, so it can
render as a real `<a href>` — and when it did, it inherited
`--cursor-button` and lost the hand that the browser gives every other
link on the page. A link styled as a button is still a link.

```css
a[href].button {
  cursor: var(--cursor-link);
}
```

The `a[href]` part is doing real work. An `<a>` without `href` is not a
link and browsers do not give it the hand either, so matching on the
attribute rather than the element keeps the rule honest.

The distinction the kit draws is navigation versus action, not
appearance: a `<button>` styled as a link would still act on the current
page, so it would keep the arrow.

| | Element | Cursor |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `<Button>` | `<button>` | arrow |
| `<Button href="/x">` | `<a href>` | hand |

The Button `Href` story asserts this, and compares against a bare
`<a href>` rather than the literal `pointer` — so overriding
`--cursor-link` moves the assertion with it instead of breaking it.

## `--cursor-disabled`

`not-allowed` — used by TextInput, and **not** by Button. That asymmetry
is not an oversight.

A disabled `<input>` stays hit-testable, so a cursor set on it renders and
the user gets feedback on hover. Button's disabled state is
`pointer-events: none`, which makes the element untargetable; an
untargetable element is never hovered, so a cursor there would be dead
CSS. The `pointer-events: none` is not incidental — because Button
can render as an `<a>`, which ignores the `disabled` attribute entirely. Blocking pointer events is what actually disables it
in that case.

So the token applies to the pattern where a control stays hoverable while
disabled — including a control deliberately wrapped so a tooltip can
explain *why*. That trade-off, between a disabled control you can
interrogate and one that is inert, is a real design choice, and the two
components here happen to sit on opposite sides of it.

## Adding tokens

A mature system ends up with a token per interactive component —
checkboxes, menu items, radios, switches, slider thumbs. This kit has
three, because it has two components and one of them can render as two
different things.

**Add a token when the component that needs it is built, not before.** A
`--cursor-slider-thumb` with no Slider is a value nobody can verify and
that the eventual Slider may not want.

## Customization

All three are plain CSS keywords, not colors, so they override like any
other custom property:

```css
:root {
  --cursor-button: pointer;
}
```

Load any override after Zweihänder's own stylesheet so the cascade picks it
up. Setting `--cursor-button: pointer` is the one-line version of adopting
the mainstream convention; it leaves `--cursor-link` alone, which is
already `pointer`, so the two simply converge.

import { Meta, Canvas, Controls } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import * as BadgeStories from './Badge.stories'

<Meta of={BadgeStories} />

# Badge

A small count or dot that flags something new on another element: unread
messages on an inbox, a status on an avatar. Spec:
[uiguideline.com/components/badge](https://www.uiguideline.com/components/badge).

<Canvas of={BadgeStories.Variants} />

## Anatomy

| Part | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **Container** | The pill. Always fully rounded, whatever the Theme's radius preset. |
| **Count** | The number, in tabular figures so `9` and `10` keep their width. |
| **Suffix "+"** | Added after `maxCount` when `count` is larger: `99+`. |
| **Dot** | `isDot`: the container with no count, for "something new" rather than "how many". |

## Props

| Prop | Values | Default | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `count` | number | – | Nothing renders without `count` or `isDot`. |
| `variant` | `primary`, `accent`, `secondary`, `destructive` | `primary` | |
| `size` | `sm`, `md` | `md` | 16px / 20px tall; dots are 6px / 8px. |
| `isDot` | boolean | `false` | |
| `maxCount` | number | – | |
| `isFloating` | boolean | `false` | Pins the badge to a corner of `children`. |
| `floatingPlacement` | `top-start`, `top-end`, `bottom-start`, `bottom-end` | `top-end` | |
| `children` | node | – | The element a floating badge sits on. |

Every other `<span>` attribute passes through to the badge.

<Controls of={BadgeStories.Default} />

### Differences from the spec

- **`children` is added.** A floating badge needs something to float on.
  The badge wraps it in a `position: relative` span rather than asking
  every consumer to position the anchor themselves.
- **`accent` is the inverted neutral.** The token set has one brand hue,
  which `primary` already uses, so `accent` is foreground-on-background:
  the strongest contrast available without inventing a colour.
- **`floatingPlacement` defaults to `top-end`**, the usual notification
  corner; the spec gives no default.
- **Start and end are physical** (left and right). RTL pages would get
  mirrored placement.

## Usage

<Canvas of={BadgeStories.Sizes} />

Use `maxCount` so a large number does not stretch the badge past its anchor.

<Canvas of={BadgeStories.MaxCount} />

A floating badge gets a ring in the page background, so it separates from
whatever it overlaps.

<Canvas of={BadgeStories.Floating} />

## Accessibility

- An **inline count** is plain text and is read where it sits. Inside a
  button it becomes part of the name ("Inbox 12").
- A **floating** badge is hidden from assistive tech: it sits *outside*
  the element it decorates, so it would be read as a stray number after
  it. Put the meaning in that element's name instead:
  `aria-label="Notifications, 4 unread"`.
- A **dot** has no text and is hidden too.
- Pass `aria-label` to any badge to expose it as an image with that name
  instead, e.g. a status dot on an avatar: `aria-label="Online"`.
- `count={0}` shows "0". Hide the badge yourself if nothing new should
  mean no badge.
- Colour is never the only signal: a destructive badge still needs words
  somewhere that say what is wrong.
- Contrast is checked by addon-a11y in error mode for every story.

import { Meta, Canvas, Controls } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import * as DividerStories from './Divider.stories'

<Meta of={DividerStories} />

# Divider

A thin line that separates content into groups: sections of a card, items
in a toolbar, blocks of a page. Spec: [uiguideline.com/components/divider](https://www.uiguideline.com/components/divider).

<Canvas of={DividerStories.Default} />

## Anatomy

One part: the **line**. It is an `<hr>`, drawn with a border in the
`--border` color, so it follows light and dark mode without extra code.

## Props

| Prop | Values | Default | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `orientation` | `horizontal`, `vertical` | `horizontal` | |
| `inset` | boolean | `false` | Indents both ends by `--space-4` (horizontal) or `--space-2` (vertical). |
| `size` | `sm`, `md`, `lg` | `sm` | Thickness: 1px, 2px, 4px. |
| `appearance` | `solid`, `dashed` | `solid` | uiguideline's `variant`. See below. |

Every other `<hr>` attribute passes through, including `ref` and `className`.

<Controls of={DividerStories.Default} />

### Differences from the spec

- **`appearance`, not `variant`.** In this kit `variant` always means a
  color by intent (primary, destructive…) and `appearance` means a style.
  Solid versus dashed is a style.
- **Thickness is raw px.** The token layer has no border-width scale, and
  a divider is the only component that needs three.

## Usage

<Canvas of={DividerStories.Sizes} />

A **vertical** divider has no fixed height: it stretches to its flex row,
which is where it almost always sits. Anywhere else, give it a height.

<Canvas of={DividerStories.Vertical} />

Use **inset** when the line sits inside a padded list and should align
with the text rather than run edge to edge.

<Canvas of={DividerStories.Inset} />

## Accessibility

- `<hr>` is announced as a separator. Vertical dividers add
  `aria-orientation="vertical"`; horizontal ones don't, because that is
  already the default.
- If the line is purely decorative, e.g. between two icons that are
  already grouped, pass `aria-hidden` so it isn't announced at all.
- The `--border` color is below 3:1 against the background on purpose: a
  divider is decoration and is not required to meet the non-text contrast
  ratio. Never let a divider be the only thing that tells groups apart.

import { Meta, Canvas, Controls } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import * as TagStories from './Tag.stories'

<Meta of={TagStories} />

# Tag

A short label that categorises or marks something: a status, a filter
chip, a person picked in a field. Spec:
[uiguideline.com/components/tag](https://www.uiguideline.com/components/tag).

<Canvas of={TagStories.Matrix} />

## Anatomy

| Part | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **Container** | The box: fill, border and corner by `appearance` and `isRounded`. |
| **Start icon** | `startIcon`, sized to the text. Decorative. |
| **Start avatar** | `startAvatar`, a small round image. Decorative (`alt=""`). Replaces the icon when both are given. |
| **Text** | `text`. Truncates with an ellipsis rather than wrapping. |
| **Remove button** | `hasRemoveButton`: a real `<button>` that calls `onRemove`. |

## Props

| Prop | Values | Default | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `text` | string | – | Required. |
| `startIcon` | node | – | Usually `<Icon name="…" />`. |
| `startAvatar` | string (URL) | – | |
| `size` | `sm`, `md` | `md` | 20px / 24px tall. |
| `appearance` | `subtle`, `outlined`, `solid` | `subtle` | |
| `variant` | `info`, `success`, `warning`, `danger` | `info` | The status tokens, see [Colors](?path=/docs/foundations-colors--docs). |
| `isRounded` | boolean | `false` | Pill, whatever the radius preset. |
| `hasRemoveButton` | boolean | `false` | |
| `onRemove` | `(event) => void` | – | |

Every other `<span>` attribute passes through to the container.

<Controls of={TagStories.Default} />

### Differences from the spec

- **The spec's four variants needed new tokens.** `info`, `success`,
  `warning` and `danger` were added to the token layer for Tag and are
  shared with Alert and Toast.
- **`startAvatar` wins over `startIcon`** if both are passed; the spec
  does not say.
- **The tag does not remove itself.** `onRemove` reports the click and
  the parent drops the tag from its list, so the list stays the one
  source of truth.

## Usage

<Canvas of={TagStories.Sizes} />

<Canvas of={TagStories.RemovableList} />

## Accessibility

- The remove button is named **"Remove {text}"**, so a list of tags does
  not read as a row of identical "Remove" buttons.
- It is a native `<button>`: Tab to reach, Enter or Space to press.
- On touch screens (`pointer: coarse`) its hit area grows to 44×44px
  without changing how the tag looks. That area reaches 10px above and
  below a 24px tag, so in a wrapped list on touch keep at least
  `--space-6` between rows, or neighbouring targets overlap and a tap can
  remove the wrong tag.
- After a tag is removed, focus has nowhere to stay. If that matters, move
  it to the next tag's remove button, or to the field the tags belong to,
  in your `onRemove`.
- Colour carries meaning here, so it must never be the only signal: the
  text says what the status is. The icon and the avatar are decorative.
- All label and text pairs clear 4.5:1 in both themes; the build checks
  them.

import { Meta, Canvas, Controls } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import * as ButtonStories from './Button.stories'

<Meta of={ButtonStories} />

# Button

Triggers an action on the current page — or, with `href`, navigates.
Spec: [uiguideline.com/components/button](https://www.uiguideline.com/components/button).

<Canvas of={ButtonStories.Matrix} />

## Anatomy

| Part | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **Container** | The box. Fill, border and label colour come from `variant` × `appearance`. |
| **Start icon** / **End icon** | `startIcon`, `endIcon`. Decorative; sized to the button. |
| **Label** | `children`. With `isIconOnly`, the icon is the whole content. |
| **Spinner** | Replaces the content while `isLoading`, without changing the width. |

## Props

| Prop | Values | Default | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `variant` | `primary`, `accent`, `secondary`, `destructive` | `primary` | Colour by meaning. |
| `appearance` | `contained`, `outlined`, `ghost` | `contained` | |
| `size` | `sm`, `md`, `lg`, `xl` | `md` | 32, 40, 48, 56px. |
| `startIcon`, `endIcon` | node | – | Usually `<Icon name="…" />`. |
| `isIconOnly` | boolean | `false` | Square. **Requires `aria-label`** (a type error without it). |
| `isLoading` | boolean | `false` | |
| `isFullWidth` | boolean | `false` | |
| `disabled` | boolean | `false` | |
| `type` | `button`, `submit`, `reset` | `button` | |
| `href` | string | – | Renders `<a>`. `target` and `rel` pass through. |
| `render` | element or function | – | Replaces the element, e.g. a router's `<Link />`. |
| `onClick` | function | – | |

Every other `<button>` attribute passes through, including `ref`.

<Controls of={ButtonStories.Default} />

### Differences from the spec

- **`disabled`, not `isDisabled`** — the native attribute keeps its name.
- **`isIconOnly` is added.** The spec has no icon-only button, and a
  square button that still requires a name is common enough to need one.
- **`render` is added** for composition with routers and other elements,
  matching Base UI and shadcn. It replaced `asChild` in 0.8.
- **`accent` is the inverted neutral** (foreground on background), as on
  Badge: the token set has one brand hue and `primary` uses it.
- Outlined and ghost `primary` use `--primary-text`, a step of the accent
  measured to read at 4.5:1 on the page. The solid step would not, for
  warm accents.

## Usage

One `primary contained` button per view: the thing to do next. Everything
else steps down to `outlined` or `ghost`, or to `secondary`.

<Canvas of={ButtonStories.Sizes} />

<Canvas of={ButtonStories.WithIcons} />

<Canvas of={ButtonStories.IconOnly} />

**Loading** keeps the button's width and focus and blocks it from acting
again, so a double-submit is impossible and a keyboard user is not dropped
back to the top of the page.

<Canvas of={ButtonStories.Loading} />

**A link is not a button.** `href` renders a real `<a>`: it keeps link
semantics, opens in a new tab on middle-click, and gets the link cursor.
Use it for navigation, and a plain Button for actions.

<Canvas of={ButtonStories.Href} />

## Accessibility

- A native `<button>`, `type="button"` by default so it never submits a
  form by accident. Enter and Space both activate it.
- `isIconOnly` needs `aria-label`; TypeScript refuses it without one.
  Icons are `aria-hidden` everywhere else, so they never double the name.
- `isLoading` sets `aria-busy` and `aria-disabled` but keeps the button
  focusable. `disabled` removes it from the tab order, as native buttons
  do.
- A disabled or loading link renders a bare `<a>` with no `href` — the
  only thing that stops an `<a>` navigating — and `aria-disabled`. With
  `render`, the render element is dropped too, since a router's Link would
  keep its own `href`.
- `render` is for elements that are already interactive: a link or a
  router's Link. It merges props onto the element and adds no role or
  keyboard handling, so do not render a `<div>` through it.
- Hover and pressed keep the label at 4.5:1 too. The `StateContrast`
  story measures every variant × appearance × state under all seventeen
  accents in both modes, from the CSS that ships.
- `sm` and `md` are under 44px; on touch screens (`pointer: coarse`) the
  hit area grows to 44×44px without the button growing.
- Focus ring: 2px `--ring`, 2px offset, at 3:1 or better on the page.

import { Meta, Canvas, Controls } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import * as ToggleButtonStories from './ToggleButton.stories'

<Meta of={ToggleButtonStories} />

# Toggle Button

A button that stays pressed: bold on or off, following or not, a filter
applied or not. Spec:
[uiguideline.com/components/toggle-button](https://www.uiguideline.com/components/toggle-button).
Behaviour from Base UI's [Toggle](https://base-ui.com/react/components/toggle);
the look is [Button](?path=/docs/components-buttons-button--docs)'s.

<Canvas of={ToggleButtonStories.Matrix} />

## Anatomy

The same parts as Button — **container**, **start icon**, **label**, **end
icon**, **spinner** — plus one state: **pressed**.

| State | Looks like |
| --- | --- |
| Unpressed | Always neutral: `secondary outlined` (or `ghost` when the appearance is ghost). |
| Pressed, `contained` | The variant's solid fill. |
| Pressed, `outlined` | The variant's border on the neutral secondary fill. |
| Pressed, `ghost` | The neutral secondary fill. |

## Props

| Prop | Values | Default | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `pressed` | boolean | – | Controlled. The spec's `isSelected`. |
| `defaultPressed` | boolean | `false` | Uncontrolled starting state. |
| `onPressedChange` | `(pressed) => void` | – | |
| `variant` | `primary`, `accent`, `secondary`, `destructive` | `primary` | Colour of the pressed state. |
| `appearance` | `contained`, `outlined`, `ghost` | `contained` | Style of the pressed state. |
| `size` | `sm`, `md`, `lg`, `xl` | `md` | |
| `startIcon`, `endIcon` | node | – | |
| `isIconOnly` | boolean | `false` | Requires `aria-label`. |
| `isLoading` | boolean | `false` | |
| `isFullWidth` | boolean | `false` | |
| `disabled` | boolean | `false` | |
| `onClick` | function | – | |

<Controls of={ToggleButtonStories.Default} />

### Differences from the spec

- **`pressed`, `defaultPressed`, `onPressedChange`** instead of
  `isSelected`: Base UI's names, per the kit's convention for components
  built on it. "Pressed" is also the ARIA word (`aria-pressed`).
- **`disabled`**, not `isDisabled`.
- **`variant` and `appearance` describe the pressed state.** The spec
  applies them to the button without saying what changes when it is
  selected. If unpressed also took them, a contained toggle would look
  pressed whether it was or not.
- **A pressed outlined or ghost toggle is filled neutral, not tinted with
  its variant.** It stays in that state indefinitely, so its label has to
  pass 4.5:1 on the fill — and red text on a red tint measures 3.7:1.
- **`isIconOnly`**, as on Button.

## Usage

Use a toggle for a setting that is on or off and applies immediately.
If the choice is submitted with a form, use a Checkbox or Switch instead.
For one-of-many, use a group of radios or tabs.

<Canvas of={ToggleButtonStories.IconOnly} />

<Canvas of={ToggleButtonStories.Controlled} />

## Accessibility

- A native `<button>` with `aria-pressed`, so a screen reader announces
  "Subscribe, toggle button, pressed".
- **Keep the label the same in both states.** `aria-pressed` carries the
  state; a label that switches from "Follow" to "Unfollow" as well reads
  as "Unfollow, pressed", which contradicts itself.
- Enter and Space both toggle it.
- `isLoading` keeps it focusable but inert, as on Button.
- 44×44px touch target at `sm` and `md`, from Button.

import { Meta, Canvas, Controls } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import * as CheckboxStories from './Checkbox.stories'

<Meta of={CheckboxStories} />

# Checkbox

Selects an option, or several from a list, to apply when a form is
submitted. Spec:
[uiguideline.com/components/checkbox](https://www.uiguideline.com/components/checkbox).
Behaviour from Base UI's [Checkbox](https://base-ui.com/react/components/checkbox)
and [Field](https://base-ui.com/react/components/field).

<Canvas of={CheckboxStories.Variants} />

## Anatomy

| Part | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **Container** | The 16px box: `--control-border` outline, filled with the variant when checked. |
| **Check icon** | `check` when checked, `minus` when indeterminate. |
| **Label** | `label`. Clicking it toggles the box. |
| **Helper text** | `helperText`, indented under the label. |

## Props

| Prop | Values | Default | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `checked` | boolean | – | Controlled. |
| `defaultChecked` | boolean | `false` | Uncontrolled. |
| `onCheckedChange` | `(checked) => void` | – | The spec's `onChange`. |
| `isIndeterminate` | boolean | `false` | |
| `label` | node | – | |
| `helperText` | node | – | |
| `name` | string | – | |
| `value` | string | `"on"` | Submitted under `name` when checked. The spec's `defaultValue`. |
| `variant` | `primary`, `secondary`, `neutral` | `neutral` | Colour of the checked box. |
| `disabled`, `required`, `readOnly`, `autoFocus` | boolean | `false` | |
| `validationState` | `default`, `success`, `error` | `default` | |

<Controls of={CheckboxStories.Default} />

### Differences from the spec

- **Base UI's and HTML's names:** `defaultChecked` and `onCheckedChange`
  for the spec's `defaultValue` (a string there, which reads as the
  submitted value — that is `value`) and `onChange`; native `disabled`,
  `required`, `readOnly` for the `is…` forms.
- **`isIndeterminate` keeps its prefix.** Indeterminate is a DOM property,
  not an HTML attribute, so by the kit's naming rule it takes `is`; Base UI
  calls it `indeterminate`.
- **`autoFocus` is applied on mount by the component.** The box is a
  focusable `<span>`, which React's own `autoFocus` ignores.
- **`neutral` is the foreground colour**, `secondary` a light fill that
  keeps its outline. The spec's variant set differs from Switch's; both
  are kept as specified.

## Usage

<Canvas of={CheckboxStories.SelectAll} />

**Indeterminate** is for a parent whose children are partly selected. It
is a display state: clicking the parent chooses all or none, never
"mixed".

<Canvas of={CheckboxStories.Validation} />

## Accessibility

- `role="checkbox"` with `aria-checked` (`mixed` when indeterminate);
  Space toggles it. The label wraps the box, so it names it and is part
  of the click target.
- The unchecked outline is `--control-border`, 3:1 on the page on every
  gray ramp.
- `helperText` is the description; the error state sets `aria-invalid`.
- A hidden native input carries `name`, `value` and `required` into form
  submission and validation.
- 44×44px touch target on coarse pointers.

import { Meta, Canvas, Controls } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'
import * as ColorPickerStories from './ColorPicker.stories'

<Meta of={ColorPickerStories} />

# Color Picker

Choose a colour: type its hex, pick from a set of swatches, or find it on
a saturation/brightness area and a hue strip. Spec:
[uiguideline.com/components/color-picker](https://www.uiguideline.com/components/color-picker).
Two exports: `ColorPicker`, a text field with a swatch button that opens
the picker in a Base UI Popover, and `ColorPanel`, the picker on its own.

<Canvas of={ColorPickerStories.Swatches} />

## Anatomy

| Part | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **Field** | A text field holding the hex, with the label, helper and validation of every Zweihänder field. |
| **Swatch button** | At the start of the field, filled with the current colour. Opens the panel. |
| **Area** | Saturation left to right, brightness bottom to top, in the current hue. |
| **Hue strip** | A slider round the colour wheel, 0 to 359 degrees. |
| **Swatches** | Optional presets. The chosen one has a ring. |

## Props

`ColorPicker`:

| Prop | Values | Default | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `value` | `#rrggbb` | – | Controlled. |
| `defaultValue` | `#rrggbb` | `#3b82f6` | |
| `onValueChange` | `(hex) => void` | – | On every change: typing (once committed), dragging, keys, swatches. |
| `swatches` | `(string \| { value, label })[]` | – | A plain string is named by its hex; give brand colours a `label`. |
| `label`, `helperText`, `validationState`, `size`, `appearance`, `isFullWidth`, `required`, `disabled` | | | As Text Input. `required` is set on the hex input. |
| `name` | string | – | Submits the hex. |

`ColorPanel` takes `value`, `defaultValue`, `onValueChange`, `swatches`,
`disabled` and `className`.

`normalizeHex(text)` is exported too: it turns `#abc`, `ABC` or `#AABBCC`
into `#aabbcc`, and anything else into `null`.

<Controls of={ColorPickerStories.Default} />

### Design notes

- **Hex in, hex out.** The value is always lowercase `#rrggbb`. Typed
  text is read on Enter or blur and accepts three or six digits, with or
  without `#`; anything else shows "Enter a colour as #rrggbb" and keeps
  the last good value.
- **The hue is remembered.** Internally the picker keeps hue, saturation
  and brightness. Drag to black and back and the hue strip stays where it
  was, instead of jumping to red as a hex round trip would.
- **No alpha, no other formats.** Opacity and RGB/HSL input are not in
  this version.
- **Thumbs read on any colour.** A white ring with a dark edge: one of
  the two is at least 3:1 against whatever is under it.

## Usage

<Canvas of={ColorPickerStories.Default} />

<Canvas of={ColorPickerStories.Panel} />

<Canvas of={ColorPickerStories.Disabled} />

## Accessibility

- The field is a text input named by its label; the swatch button is
  named "Choose colour, #3b82f6 selected", and the popup is a dialog
  named "Choose colour" that returns focus to the button on Escape.
- The area is one tab stop: a slider named "Saturation" whose value text
  reads both numbers ("Saturation 76%, brightness 96%"). Left and right
  change saturation, up and down brightness, Shift moves 10%, Page Up/Down
  change brightness by 10%, Home and End set saturation to 0 or 100%.
  A second "Brightness" slider is there for a screen reader's browse mode.
- The hue strip is a Base UI slider named "Hue", read as "217 degrees".
- Swatches are native radios in a radio group named "Swatches": one tab
  stop, arrows move and choose, and the chosen one is checked. None is
  checked while the colour is not one of them. They are 24px with 8px
  between them, which meets WCAG 2.5.8 without an invisible larger
  target.
- A colour is never the only way to know the value: the hex is always in
  the field.

<Meta of={RadioStories} />

# Radio

Chooses exactly one option from a short list, all visible at once. Spec:
[uiguideline.com/components/radio](https://www.uiguideline.com/components/radio).
Behaviour from Base UI's [Radio Group](https://base-ui.com/react/components/radio),
[Field](https://base-ui.com/react/components/field) and
[Fieldset](https://base-ui.com/react/components/fieldset).

<Canvas of={RadioStories.Default} />

## Anatomy

| Part | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **Legend** | `label`: names the group. |
| **Radio** | The 16px circle: `--control-border` outline, filled with the variant and a dot when selected. |
| **Option label** | Each option's `label`. Clicking it selects the option. |
| **Option helper** | Each option's `helperText`, indented under its label. |
| **Group helper** | `helperText` under the group: the error message when `validationState` is error. |

## Props

The component is `RadioGroup`.

| Prop | Values | Default | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `options` | `{ value, label, helperText?, disabled? }[]` | – | Required. |
| `label` | node | – | The legend. |
| `helperText` | node | – | |
| `value` | string | – | Controlled. |
| `defaultValue` | string | – | |
| `onValueChange` | `(value) => void` | – | The spec's `onChange`. |
| `name` | string | – | |
| `variant` | `primary`, `secondary`, `neutral` | `neutral` | |
| `orientation` | `vertical`, `horizontal` | `vertical` | Layout only; arrow keys work either way. |
| `disabled`, `required`, `readOnly` | boolean | `false` | |
| `validationState` | `default`, `success`, `error` | `default` | |

<Controls of={RadioStories.Default} />

### Differences from the spec

- **The component is the group.** The spec describes a single radio, but
  a radio means nothing alone: selection, arrow keys and the single tab
  stop all belong to the group. Following the kit's "flat props"
  convention, the radios are `options` rather than child components.
- **`checked` and `autoFocus` per radio are not props.** The group's
  `value` says which is checked.
- Base UI's `onValueChange` and native `disabled`, `required`,
  `readOnly` names, as on Checkbox.

## Usage

Up to about six options. More than that, or options that do not fit on
screen, is a Select.

<Canvas of={RadioStories.Horizontal} />

<Canvas of={RadioStories.Validation} />

## Accessibility

- A `<fieldset>` with a `<legend>`, exposed as a `radiogroup` named by
  the legend.
- **One tab stop for the group.** Tab enters at the selected radio (or
  the first), arrow keys move and select, Tab leaves. Disabled options
  are skipped.
- Each option's helper text is its own description; the group message
  follows the group.
- The unselected outline is `--control-border`, 3:1 on the page.
- A hidden native input carries `name` and `required` into form
  submission and validation.
- 44×44px touch target on each radio on coarse pointers.

# Rating

Asks for, or shows, a score out of a few stars: a review, a template's
rating, a difficulty. Spec:
[uiguideline.com/components/rating](https://www.uiguideline.com/components/rating).
Built on native radio buttons; no Base UI part covers it.

<Canvas of={RatingStories.Default} />

## Anatomy

| Part | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **Label** | Optional legend over the stars; names the group. |
| **Star** | Filled in `--warning-text` up to the value, outlined in `--control-border` after it. 24px (16px at `sm`, 32px at `lg`). |

| Prop | Values | Default | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `value`, `defaultValue`, `onValueChange` | number | `0` | 0 is unrated. |
